title: Patterned vision from the brain when the eye cannot send signals

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a brain prosthesis that gives people useful patterned vision when their eyes or optic nerves cannot deliver visual signals. An external camera would capture a scene, and a processor would translate it into electrical stimulation of visual brain tissue. The intended result is perception organized well enough to support ordinary reading and face recognition, beyond detecting isolated spots of light called phosphenes. The supplied evidence establishes early components of this approach, but does not demonstrate that complete capability.

Cortical and thalamic implants offer related routes around damaged retinal input, with different anatomical requirements. Cortical stimulation requires healthy, accessible visual cortex and sufficient remaining circuitry to interpret the stimulation. A thalamic implant would also require usable thalamic tissue and the downstream connections that carry its signals to visual cortex. Neither approach can be assumed to restore vision when its target or necessary downstream circuitry is extensively damaged.

significance.text: When both eyes, both optic nerves, or their connections through the optic chiasm cannot transmit useful signals, an ocular treatment alone cannot restore vision unless a functional route to the brain is also preserved or rebuilt. A successful brain prosthesis would provide another route for visual information to enter the nervous system. This bypass is particularly consequential for people whose blindness cannot be addressed by repairing optical structures or stimulating surviving retinal cells.

Conditional impact assessment: reproducible ordinary reading and face recognition without usable retinal input would establish a new functional sensory channel and materially expand what visual restoration can offer. Better object recognition and independent mobility are plausible further benefits, but each requires its own demonstration. Success on print or faces would not by itself establish safe navigation through unfamiliar rooms, streets or moving crowds.

Scope and impact synthesis: useful form vision need not reproduce every property of natural sight. Natural color, coordination with gaze, a wide visual field and effective perception during movement could require further encoding and engineering advances. Retinal prostheses are an informative comparison because they demonstrate electrical substitution within the visual system, but they retain biological pathways that this innovation must bypass. Higher resolution in a retinal prosthesis falls outside this entry's scope; that boundary does not imply that every future retinal advance would be scientifically incremental.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is a reliable way to turn camera images into stimulation patterns that produce useful, interpretable spatial vision. The supplied review describes cortical stimulation that evokes phosphenes, some letters and simple shapes, while also reporting that simultaneous stimulation of multiple contacts can merge percepts into large, indistinct patches. More electrodes therefore cannot simply be assumed to provide an equivalent number of independent visual pixels. Spatial interactions between stimulated sites must be understood and controlled.

Scaling also creates a difficult encoding and computation problem. The supplied review describes a large stimulation-optimization parameter space as the number of arrays increases, with implications for producing vision quickly enough to be useful. The evidence supports these concrete challenges, but does not establish that no useful camera-to-stimulation encoding exists or directly substantiate the earlier categorical claim that current systems have too few stable, mapped percepts. The stronger defensible conclusion is that ordinary reading and face recognition through the proposed brain bypass are not demonstrated in the supplied evidence.

Engineering synthesis: a practical system would need dependable percept mapping over time, sufficiently distinct spatial information, tolerable processing delay and stimulation that remains safe during repeated everyday use. The supplied sources do not establish the safety of dense, chronic intracortical stimulation at the scale required for the proposed capability. Long follow-up of a cortical surface array cannot settle that question because surface and penetrating interfaces differ, and basic device functionality does not by itself establish durable useful vision.

current_state.text: Holz and colleagues' 2025 PRIMA study demonstrates electrical substitution through surviving inner retinal circuitry. Its photovoltaic pixels stimulate retinal bipolar cells, and information continues to the brain through the optic nerve. This provides evidence that an electronic implant can support form vision, while retaining a pathway unavailable to the population targeted by this entry.

PRIMA's reported mean native prosthetic visual acuity was logMAR 1.32 ± 0.16, equivalent to Snellen 20/417 and consistent with its 100 µm pixels. This measurement used Landolt C optotypes displayed directly through the glasses, without the camera, zoom or image processing. Camera-based digital enhancement enabled better reading performance, so 20/417 should not be treated as a ceiling on enhanced reading. The supplied review had a complete main-text manuscript, but the linked supplementary materials and videos were not supplied or inspected.

Cavaleri and colleagues' 2025 review characterizes optic-nerve, thalamic and cortical prostheses as early in development. It describes cortical demonstrations involving some letters, shapes and object boundaries, alongside the difficulty of obtaining distinct percepts from simultaneous stimulation. For thalamic stimulation, it cites visual percepts elicited by microstimulation of the lateral geniculate nucleus in non-human primates. That preliminary basis does not establish useful human vision from a thalamic prosthesis. The supplied extraction retained the review's main text but truncated during its references, which limits access to the full bibliography without undermining these retained passages.

A Medical Product Outsourcing article dated 16 March 2026 reports Cortigent's account of six-year early-feasibility results for Orion, a 60-electrode cortical surface system. According to that account, participants improved with the system on versus off when detecting a small square on a screen and detecting movement across the visual field. The article also reports device functionality over follow-up. These findings concern limited visual tasks and do not establish ordinary reading, face recognition or dense intracortical performance.

The Orion account also reports that three of six participants underwent explantation after their three-year visits and that one seizure occurred early in the study. These details limit a broad characterization of the report as demonstrating six-year safety for every participant. The findings are company-reported through a trade publication; no peer-reviewed six-year clinical report is included in the supplied material. That absence does not establish that such a publication does not exist.

The earlier research attributes to Grant and colleagues' June 2025 ARVO abstract 5758 a limitation in fine-detail perception and 35% prosthesis-only object recognition by one participant on a four-object near task. The source index contains its URL but no captured abstract, so the supplied review could verify neither the wording nor the numerical result. These remain unresolved attributed claims, not established performance estimates or evidence that the abstract's results are false.

Evidence-scope limitation: the supplied freshness record is empty. The dated findings above remain informative, but the material does not establish a comprehensive account of developments through 1 November 2026. It supports an unresolved functional goal within the supplied evidence, rather than a definitive claim that no later system has advanced beyond these reports.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: participants with no light perception and no usable optic-nerve input would read ordinary print and recognize faces using visual information supplied by the prosthesis in real rooms. Controls would need to establish that performance depends on prosthetic visual input and is not explained by residual vision or other cues. Detection of a light square or success on a simple forced-choice grating would be insufficient for this entry's intended capability. These are proposed criteria, not an established clinical standard.
completion_criteria.label: Prosthetic input enables reading ordinary print and recognizing faces

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement protocol: define print size, reading accuracy and speed, viewing distance, lighting, permitted magnification and image processing. Specify face-recognition accuracy, the number and familiarity of faces, and performance across changing viewpoints and backgrounds. Report native spatial performance separately from performance aided by digital enhancement, so improvements from encoding or magnification are interpretable. No particular acuity value, including 20/40, is required by this entry or established here as an authoritative threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Report reading and face-recognition protocols, separating native and enhanced performance

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability and reproducibility criteria: demonstrate useful function for a prospectively specified period measured in years, with transparent reporting of adverse events, device failures, explantations, recalibration and any decline in performance. Replication across participants and independent teams would strengthen confidence that results extend beyond one unusually favorable case. Report anatomical eligibility, usable visual field, latency, training requirements and assistance needed. A finite test program would establish the breadth actually demonstrated, with remaining population and environmental limits made explicit.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrate years of useful function with transparent outcomes and limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed additional outcomes: assess independent mobility, broader object recognition, natural color, gaze coordination and wider-field vision separately if these benefits are claimed. Reading and face recognition would satisfy the core functional target only under the specified controls and durability requirements; they would not automatically validate these further capabilities.
completion_criteria.label: Separately assess additional visual capabilities whenever their benefits are claimed

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OPH-01, Retinotopic reconnection of retinal ganglion cell axons to brain targets, addresses the same lost-input problem by rebuilding a biological pathway. OPH-05 instead supplies visual information downstream of the damaged eye-to-brain input. Successful reconnection could make retinal signals usable again, whereas a brain prosthesis must generate interpretable stimulation without relying on that reconnection. These are distinct restoration strategies.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-02, Biological reconstruction of foveal cones, RPE, and their blood supply; OPH-07, One programmable repair for many photoreceptor and RPE gene defects; OPH-08, Reperfusion of established retinal capillary dropout; and OPH-11, Prevention of progression from early or intermediate AMD to late AMD, address reconstruction, repair or preservation within the retina and its support systems. Their intended benefits require visual information to reach the brain through a usable pathway. OPH-05 addresses the separate situation in which ocular input cannot be transmitted, while PRIMA provides a relevant electrical-substitution comparison that still depends on surviving retinal circuitry and an optic nerve.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-03, Reversal of established cataract without removing the lens, and OPH-04, A manufactured cornea that clears vascularized stromal opacity, address optical barriers before light reaches the retina. OPH-06, A closed-loop control that sets axial eye growth, addresses eye development and geometry. These entries work on the eye's capacity to form or preserve useful input; OPH-05 introduces a downstream channel when that input cannot reach the brain.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-09, Reopening of the human visual critical period, concerns visual plasticity and could overlap with learning to interpret prosthetic input. Whether such an intervention would improve brain-prosthesis outcomes remains an open possibility, not a demonstrated dependency. OPH-10, Arrest of glaucomatous ganglion-cell death when pressure is not the lever, concerns preserving retinal output neurons. Preserving those neurons and bypassing an unusable input pathway are distinct objectives; neither entry subsumes the other.

change_log.change: Preserved OPH-05's identity as useful patterned vision delivered through a brain bypass, while explaining cortical and thalamic anatomical requirements.
change_log.reason: The review supports the concept but conditions its feasibility on usable target and downstream visual circuitry.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical claims about insufficient stable percepts and absent useful encoding with specific demonstrated limitations and evidence boundaries.
change_log.reason: The supplied review documents percept merging and scaling challenges, but does not directly establish the original blanket negative claims.

change_log.change: Clarified PRIMA's retinal mechanism, exact native-acuity result and measurement conditions, and distinguished digitally enhanced reading.
change_log.reason: Snellen 20/417 concerns direct optotype presentation without camera, zoom or processing and should not be interpreted as an enhanced-reading ceiling.

change_log.change: Expanded the Orion account to include surface-array placement, limited visual tasks, three explantations and an early seizure.
change_log.reason: These details constrain efficacy and safety interpretations and prevent extrapolation to dense chronic intracortical stimulation.

change_log.change: Retained the Grant abstract's 35% result and fine-detail limitation only as unresolved attributed claims.
change_log.reason: The abstract was not captured, so neither claim could be verified. The recommendation to remove reliance on these claims was adopted without erasing their unresolved provenance.

change_log.change: Separated core reading and face-recognition outcomes from mobility and other possible benefits, and qualified the exclusion of ocular treatments.
change_log.reason: Mobility needs separate testing, and future ocular approaches could attempt to rebuild a functional pathway.

change_log.change: Treated retinal-resolution improvements as outside this entry's scope rather than universally incremental.
change_log.reason: A concept boundary does not establish the significance of all future retinal innovations.

change_log.change: Expanded completion proposals to cover controls, measurement conditions, durability, replication and practical boundaries.
change_log.reason: The original functional goal needs operational definitions, while proposed thresholds must remain distinct from established standards.

change_log.change: Preserved source-access and freshness limitations and mapped relationships across the supplied roster.
change_log.reason: The final record must distinguish dated evidence from comprehensive currentness and explain overlap without merging separate concepts.

unresolved_issues: The uncaptured Grant abstract leaves its attributed fine-detail limitation and 35% four-object result unverified, including task conditions and statistical interpretation.
No peer-reviewed Orion six-year report is included. Independent assessment of the reported efficacy, adverse events, explantations and longitudinal function remains unavailable in this evidence set.
The supplied material does not establish safety or durable useful vision for dense chronic intracortical stimulation at the proposed scale.
The empty freshness record prevents a comprehensive currentness assessment through 1 November 2026.
PRIMA's supplementary materials and videos were not supplied or inspected, and the Cavaleri extraction truncates during the references.

Completion protocols still need numerical performance targets, specified follow-up duration, eligibility criteria and rules for permitted enhancement; this record proposes dimensions to measure without inventing consensus thresholds.
The breadth of benefit across different causes and durations of blindness, and the added contribution of visual plasticity interventions, remain undetermined.

brief.title: Useful sight when the eyes cannot send signals
possible: People whose eyes or optic nerves cannot send visual signals could read ordinary print and recognize faces through a brain implant. A camera would capture the scene, and a processor would turn it into electrical signals delivered to brain tissue involved in vision.
why: This would give visual information another route into the brain for people whom eye treatments cannot help. Reading and recognizing faces would establish a useful new sensory channel, expanding what restoring sight can mean.

sources.showed: Their review describes brain stimulation that produces spots of light, some letters and simple shapes. Stimulating several sites together can blur these perceptions into indistinct patches.
sources.quote: Additionally, retinal neuroprosthetics have shown efficacy in restoring functional vision, and neuroprosthetic devices targeting the optic nerve, thalamus, and cortex are in early stages of development.
sources.cited_for: Brain stimulation can produce simple visual perceptions, but assembling them into useful spatial vision remains difficult.
sources.not_established: The work does not establish ordinary reading or face recognition through a brain implant.

sources.showed: In a small clinical study, the PRIMA implant improved central vision in people with age-related damage to the retina, the eye’s light-sensitive tissue. Digital enhancement helped reading.
sources.quote: There was no significant change in peripheral natural VA compared to baseline.
sources.cited_for: An electronic implant can support recognition of visual forms through surviving eye-to-brain connections.
sources.not_established: PRIMA still needs a working optic nerve, so it does not demonstrate the brain bypass.

sources.showed: This conference abstract concerns fine-detail perception and object recognition with a visual prosthesis.
sources.cited_for: The abstract concerns the ability to perceive detail and recognize objects with a prosthesis.
sources.not_established: A limited object-recognition task cannot establish ordinary reading or face recognition.

sources.who: Cortigent and the Orion study investigators
sources.showed: Cortigent reported better square and movement detection with Orion switched on. The small study also reported device removals and a seizure.
sources.quote: After training and experience using the Orion system, all subjects demonstrated improvement with the system turned on versus off in visual function tests to detect a small square on a computer screen and detect movement across the visual field.
sources.cited_for: An implant on the brain’s surface can support limited visual detection tasks.
sources.not_established: These company-reported results do not establish reading, face recognition or the safety of densely packed electrodes penetrating brain tissue.

shown: Brain implants have produced spots of light, some letters and simple shapes. Cortigent’s small Orion study reported improved detection of squares and movement. Useful everyday reading and face recognition through a brain bypass remain undemonstrated.
missing: Camera images still need to produce distinct, interpretable visual patterns reliably, without stimulated spots merging together.
A practical system still needs stable perceptions, tolerable delay and safe stimulation during repeated everyday use.
Reading and face recognition still need convincing demonstrations in people without usable signals from their eyes.

milestones.label: Ordinary reading and face recognition through the implant
milestones.explanation: People with no light perception or usable optic-nerve input would have to read print and recognize faces in real rooms, with other cues ruled out. This would establish useful patterned vision.

milestones.label: Clear measurements with and without digital enhancement
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to report reading speed and accuracy, face-recognition conditions, and performance with and without magnification or image processing. This would distinguish basic visual detail from gains due to enhancement.

milestones.label: Years of useful function with openly reported limits
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to show useful vision over years, report harms, failures and support needs, and reproduce results across people and teams. This would establish durability and the range of people and settings helped.

milestones.label: Separate demonstrations of any further visual benefits
milestones.explanation: Any claimed benefits for mobility, object recognition, color, coordination with gaze or wider vision would need separate tests. Reading and face recognition alone would not establish these abilities.

uncertain: The required performance levels, follow-up length and permitted digital enhancement still need to be defined.
Benefit may depend on the cause and duration of blindness and on how much usable visual brain tissue remains.
The safety of long-term stimulation through densely packed electrodes inside brain tissue remains unresolved.

page.title: Brain-based visual prostheses for form vision
page.definition: A camera-driven brain implant supplies form vision—the perception of spatial shapes—when the eyes or optic nerves cannot transmit visual information. Stimulation of visual cortex or the lateral geniculate nucleus, the thalamic relay to cortex, supports large-print reading, face and object identification, and walking navigation.

goal.need: WHO counts 7.7 million people with glaucoma-related distance vision impairment or blindness among people whose vision impairment is preventable or unaddressed. Brain prostheses target a subset of profound blindness by bypassing damaged eyes and optic nerves. The 7.7 million figure describes disease burden; it does not estimate implant eligibility.

statements.body: NIH Advisory Committee to the Director, BRAIN Initiative Working Group
statements.quote: it should be possible to devise intelligent retinal or cortical prostheses or other devices to restore sight.
Orion is intended to provide artificial vision to people who are profoundly blind
statements.context: Orion is Cortigent's investigational cortical visual prosthesis. The statement appears in its filing of 13 May 2026.

completion.title: A brain visual prosthesis meets CRMRP's reading, recognition and walking-navigation target.
completion.criterion: A cortical or thalamic prototype enables walking navigation, identification of faces and objects needed in daily life, and large-print reading, and is economically feasible. The programme supplies no numerical clinical-performance or cost pass limits.
completion.set_by: U.S. Army Clinical and Rehabilitative Medicine Research Program (CRMRP), MTEC solicitation 16-02, section 3.2.1.
completion.threshold_quote: identify faces and objects critical to daily life, and read large print
completion.basis: The programme explicitly covers both brain targets and names these functions. It supplies a capability specification rather than an operational clinical success protocol.

milestones.title: Brain stimulation reaches a 50% phosphene-detection threshold in non-human primates.
milestones.criterion: Reach a finite current at which an animal detects a stimulation-induced visual percept on 50% of presentations, the C50 detection convention. Cortical result: in 2020, two sighted macaques received 1,024-electrode implants; C50 was assessed on 184 and 164 primary visual cortex electrodes. Thalamic result: in 2007, two sighted macaques made eye movements to electrically generated visual targets; that paper did not report a C50 estimate.
milestones.set_by: Psychophysical C50 convention, applied by Chen and colleagues in monkeys and Fernández and colleagues in humans. Chen's published animal protocol concerned visual cortex.
milestones.threshold_quote: defined as the level at which the monkey reported the phosphene 50% of the time

milestones.title: A brain implant elicits visual percepts at measured stimulation thresholds in a blind participant.
milestones.criterion: Elicit visual percepts and estimate stimulation thresholds during the registered implantation period, up to 6 months. The published CORTIVIS implementation defines threshold as 50% detection probability and includes sham stimulation. Published on 19 October 2021, the cortical study implanted 96 electrodes in one participant for 6 months; 88 electrodes elicited phosphenes, with mean threshold 66.8 ± 36.5 μA. No human thalamic implantation result was located.
milestones.set_by: CORTIVIS registered protocol NCT02983370 and its published methods; the protocol was written for cortical implantation.
milestones.threshold_quote: amplitude value at 50% probability of detection

milestones.title: A brain-prosthesis user identifies grating orientation with at least 80% accuracy over 8 or more trials.
milestones.criterion: Pass the Berkeley Rudimentary Vision Test's two-choice grating task with at least 80% correct across at least 8 presentations; grating cards are presented at 25 cm. Related cortical evidence published on 14 May 2020 involved 2 blind and 3 sighted participants: one blind participant identified 33 of 36 directly stimulated three-choice forms at 30 forms/minute. This was not a Berkeley test or camera-based reading. No corresponding human thalamic result was located.
milestones.set_by: International HOVER Taskforce, 2020 consensus recommendations, Berkeley Rudimentary Vision Test protocol; applicable across vision-restoration approaches.
milestones.threshold_quote: successful identification is taken as 80% or more correct responses across eight or more presentations

milestones.title: Camera-driven brain stimulation improves square localisation with the system on versus off at p<0.05.
milestones.criterion: Square-localisation error is lower with the camera-driven system on than off, using the Orion study's t-test criterion p<0.05. Cortigent's filing of 13 May 2026 reports improvement in all 5 tested cortical recipients at 36 months. These are company-reported results, not peer reviewed. Six people were implanted; three completed 6-year follow-up, three were explanted after their 3-year visits and one at study end. One early seizure occurred. No human thalamic result was located.
milestones.set_by: Second Sight's Orion early-feasibility study, published 2019 study presentation; the criterion was written for a cortical prosthesis.
milestones.threshold_quote: Mean error significantly different ON vs. OFF, t-test, p<0.05

milestones.title: A brain prosthesis provides central 20/40-equivalent stimulation density and 70° peripheral coverage.
milestones.criterion: Provide stimulation density equivalent to at least Snellen 20/40 in the central 2° and peripheral coverage equivalent to at least 70° horizontally per eye. These are engineering equivalents, not measured perceptual acuity. No opened human report establishes both specifications for either case.
milestones.threshold_quote: Provides density of stimulation for the equivalent of at least 20/40

not_found: No operational clinical pass limits for the complete CRMRP functional target were found in the programme specification, HOVER recommendations or searched trial records.
No human thalamic visual-prosthesis implantation result was located.
No clinical report demonstrating the combined reading, identification and walking-navigation target was located.
ClinicalTrials.gov study pages returned no readable study details when opened, although indexed protocol text was available.
The supplied Grant ARVO abstract, NEJM PRIMA article and Medical Product Outsourcing Orion article could not be opened.
No peer-reviewed six-year Orion clinical report could be opened; a 2026 conference abstract was located.
No final Orion pivotal-trial safety and efficacy thresholds were found.
